summary: Discovery focused on StrataCore's reserved GPU needs and evaluation of an on‑prem/private path. Main concerns: isolation and noisy neighbor risk, burst handling (prewarm / warm pools), SLOs vs cost tradeoffs, and compliance (KMS/audit/SAML). Agreement to share sizing worksheet, SOC2 + private deployment checklist, and to run a benchmark window on reserved nodes.
topics: Burst strategy: warm vs hot pools
transcript:
[00:00] Michael (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we have about 45 minutes carved out. Quick intros?
[00:08] Jordan (CTO): Jordan here, CTO at StrataCore — we run a real‑time document processing stack, lots of short requests, occasional heavy batch reindexing.
[00:15] Aisha (SRE): Aisha — we own infra and ops, want to understand isolation/eviction risk.
[00:22] Michael: Great. Sarah, Diego from our side?
[00:25] Sarah (SE): Yep hi all, I'm Sarah, SE — I'll walk through how Dedicated works, prewarm options, and the on‑prem path.
[00:30] Ben (Infra): Ben here — main ask is predictable latency under burst and compliance constraints.
[00:34] Michael: Perfect. So high level: are you leaning hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[00:40] Jordan: We're evaluating three lanes. For production we want reserved capacity — predictable throughput. But we also need a path to on‑prem for sensitive PII workloads. So Dedicated + Private-ish.
[00:52] Sarah: Makes sense. For reserved GPUs you commit to a pool, we allocate isolated nodes or tenant‑fenced slices depending on the config. Could you share your 95/99th latency SLOs and burst patterns?
[01:05] Jordan: Sure. Our SLO is 99th < 350ms for short chat completions (<=512 tokens). But spikes from batch jobs push requests concurrently; peak QPS can triple baseline for 2‑4 minutes, maybe twice a day.
[01:20] Aisha: Also, we can't have cross‑tenant noisy neighbor impact for a certain customer set — legal requires stronger isolation for them.
[01:28] Sarah: Right, we have options: dedicated nodes pinned to you (full isolation), or reserved pools with tenant fencing and preemption policies. Full isolated nodes remove noisy neighbor but increase cost.
[01:40] Michael: To be clear on terminology — 'Dedicated' in our offering can be either reserved shared pool or fully isolated racks for an enterprise. On‑prem path means a private control plane and customer‑owned hardware.
[01:52] Ben: For on‑prem, how much of the Redwood control plane stays in Redwood? Are we comfortable with the data plane being in our VPC?
[02:00] Diego: For Private deployments we offer customer‑managed network, control plane can be private, and you can plug HSM/KMS. There is still some telemetry hooks we need for health but those can be restricted.
[02:12] Maya (Security): Quick on compliance: SOC 2? Audit log retention? KMS/HSM integration and key custody?
[02:19] Michael: We are SOC 2 certified; we'll send the report. For keys we support both customer‑managed KMS and HSM integrations in Private. Audit logs can be forwarded and retained per contract.
[02:30] Jordan: Good. Can you walk us through burst strategy — warm vs hot pool — and how that affects cost and cold latency?
[02:38] Sarah: Sure. Hot pools are prewarmed VMs/GPU instances always sitting with model loaded — fastest but expensive. Warm pools hold cached KV entries and partially loaded models — faster than cold but cheaper. We also do prefix caching and dynamic batching to improve token throughput.
[02:54] Aisha: With warm pools, what's the typical cold start penalty?
[02:58] Sarah: Depends on model size and quantization. For a 13B model quantized to 4‑bit, warm->hot transition can be ~200‑400ms. Cold spin up (from scratch) could be multiple seconds. Important to size your warm pool to cover expected spike concurrency.
[03:13] Ben: Our peaks are short — 2‑4 minutes — so we don't want to keep a giant hot pool on standby. Is there a hybrid where we prewarm some capacity and allow burst to hosted fallback?
[03:23] Sarah: Yes — smart routing allows you to fall back to a lower‑cost hosted variant during extreme spikes, or to spill to a different region. That's a policy you can configure per endpoint.
[03:33] Jordan: We also care about model version pinning during rollouts — can't have inconsistent outputs mid‑migration.
[03:38] Diego: We support model pinning and can orchestrate canary rollouts across your dedicated nodes. KV cache invalidation is handled with controlled cache draining.
[03:46] Jordan: How about preemption and eviction — do reserved nodes ever get preempted for higher tier customers?
[03:51] Michael: For fully isolated reserved racks, we don't preempt. For shared reserved pools there are tiered policies — but we can set fallback models or routing. We'll document eviction SLAs.
[04:02] Aisha: What's the typical utilization you see customers run at? We want cost-efficiency but predictable latencies.
[04:08] Sarah: Most teams run 40‑70% average utilization and size for 60‑80% to have headroom for spikes with warm pools. We can run a sim using your traffic profile to recommend exact numbers.
[04:19] Jordan: Speaking of sim — we'll share a day's worth of traffic and a synthetic spike profile. Can you run test benchmarks on reserved nodes?
[04:25] Michael: Yes, we can provision a benchmark window — usually 48–72 hours — with dedicated nodes and run your traffic to measure latency and cost. There are two flavors: hosted-backed reserved pool or on‑prem reserved nodes. Both work.
[04:37] Ben: For on‑prem provisioning, what's the lead time for hardware and deployment?
[04:41] Sarah: If you're providing hardware it can be days to a week for software deployment; if Redwood ships hardware through partners it's usually 4–8 weeks including procurement.
[04:49] Maya: Encryption at rest/in transit? We need to ensure keys are customer controlled for certain datasets.
[04:53] Diego: We support TLS for transit, and you can enforce customer KMS for encryption at rest. For HSM we integrate with common providers; we'll include our Private deployment KMS diagram.
[05:03] Jordan: Costs — curious about how warm pools affect unit economics; do you have a model?
[05:07] Michael: We'll share a warm‑pool cost model. Roughly, warm pools cost ~35‑60% of hot pools depending on model size and how much of the model you pin residency for. There's also the caching/batching efficiency which reduces per‑token compute.
[05:20] Aisha: Any limitations on GPU type for private? We plan to use A100s, maybe H100s later.
[05:26] Sarah: We support A100 and H100; kernel selection and quantization differ but runtime supports both. On‑prem we can certify specific hardware during onboarding.
[05:35] Ben: For noisy neighbor, you mentioned tenant fencing; can you expand?
[05:38] Sarah: Tenant fencing uses software isolation at the scheduler level and can combine with dedicated GPUs per tenant. It limits blast radius — if one tenant saturates memory or network we can throttle or isolate. It's not as strict as physical isolation but cheaper.
[05:50] Jordan: For our high‑risk customers we probably need physical isolation. For others tenant fencing is fine.
[05:55] Michael: Makes sense to mix tiers.
[05:57] Maya: We need audit logs with immutable retention and the ability to forward to our SIEM. Does Redwood support that for Private?
[06:04] Diego: Yes, logs can be forwarded to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) and retention is contract configurable. Immutable retention and tailing is part of our enterprise package.
[06:13] Jordan: On the topic of model artifacts, do you store model weights or do we bring them?
[06:17] Sarah: You can bring weights or we can host them in a private model registry. For private deployments, the registry can be on your network.
[06:25] Ben: Ok. I have one ops question — autoscaling and burst: how quickly can you scale out GPU capacity?
[06:31] Sarah: For warm pools scaling is near‑instant because instances are prewarmed. For cold scale out it's minutes. If you need sub‑second scale we advise prewarmed hot capacity or hosted fallback.
[06:42] Jordan: Any limitations on concurrent KV cache size? We have long contexts for some workflows — 8k tokens sometimes.
[06:48] Sarah: KV cache sizing is configurable; larger contexts increase memory and reduce batch sizes. We'll include a recommendation based on your context length distribution.
[06:58] Aisha: On observability — token‑level cost, per‑route latency, traces?
[07:02] Diego: Redwood Console exposes token cost breakdowns, per‑route dashboards, traces and error rates. For private we can route metrics to your workspace as well.
[07:10] Jordan: Any open security concerns customers often hit during on‑prem?
[07:14] Maya: We worry about OS patch windows and supply chain — how do you vet images?
[07:18] Diego: We provide hardened images and can run or accept your SBOM checks. For on‑prem, image signing and SBOM are standard.
[07:26] Michael: We're close to time — quick recap and next steps?
[07:30] Jordan: Recap — we want a sizing recommendation for reserved nodes, an estimate for hybrid warm pool + fallback, SOC2 docs, and a benchmark window.
[07:38] Michael: Action items noted — we'll send worksheet and SOC2, Sarah will prepare benchmark plan.
[07:42] Ben: We'll pull together traffic profile and compliance Qs.
[07:45] Aisha: Schedule ops deep dive next week — two hours.
[07:48] Michael: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the artifacts.
[07:52] [call ends]
